title: Chapter 2 — The Moral Economies of Conversion
paragraphs: Chapter 2 turns from exchange to religion and asks why Samoan migrants convert from one form of Christianity to another — typically leaving mainline Samoan churches (Catholic, Congregational/EFKS) for evangelical, Pentecostal, Mormon, or Seventh-Day Adventist churches. Gershon's key move: these conversions are not changes of doctrine or moral order. Many converts happily attend a mainline church in the morning and an evangelical one in the afternoon. What changes is their reflexive stance toward a moral order — they are moving between moral economies.

By "moral economy" she means more than the moral assumptions behind economic life; she means the particular reflexive stance a moral order requires you to adopt. Her interlocutors never spoke of "stances," though — they spoke of meaningful versus meaningless worship. When people called mainline Samoan worship "meaningless," Gershon reads them as rejecting the stance that church demanded; and once worship can be called meaningless, cultural practices like ritual exchange can be reframed as empty too. "Meaning" is how people feel connected to a moral order.

She admits she gathered this material by accident, while interviewing mixed-marriage couples, when the question "How did you receive the Lord into your life?" unlocked rich conversion narratives. As a Jewish interviewer she was an outsider, which shaped the testimony-to-a-nonbeliever tone. Her main site was a Pentecostal congregation meeting Sunday afternoons in a West Auckland gym — a literal "muscular Christianity" of mirrors and mats, mostly New-Zealand-raised Samoans, young families, and job-training connections.

Gershon narrates her own analytical mistake. She kept explaining conversion in rational-choice terms: evangelical churches simply cost less, since they don't demand the constant public contributions of the mainline churches. Her interlocutors politely refused this. The issue, they insisted, was meaningless worship, not money — and their vivid, physical accounts of encountering Christ resisted her sociological reading. She concludes the economic explanation is too thin: conversion is about the moral self one fashions, not about doctrine or cost.

A key informant, Sara (mother of Lotu), taught her two weighty words: power and pride. Pride, with its partner shame, is almost the only motive Samoans attribute to other people's giving in fa’alavelave; but when describing their own giving they speak of alofa — respectful love — and family obligation. Drawing on Shore, Gershon explains Samoan personhood as sociocentric: the self is activated by context and others' gazes, and "a misdeed is not a misdeed until publicly known." There is no private morality.

Diaspora strains that sociocentric morality, which needs both cultural fluency and the right public settings — both scarce abroad. Evangelical churches offer an alternative: anonymous, free-will offerings (bags no one can see into) instead of the deacon's public reading of each family's donation. The shift is from a faith that is exhibited to one that is emoted — from being worshipful without visible effort to achieving and revealing the labour of a moral self. Converts move from a context-dependent (cultural) self toward a continuous, self-monitoring (acultural) one; couples like Thomas & Sina, under Mormon rules against exchanging fine mats, refocus on the nuclear family. The burden of fa’alavelave, Gershon stresses, is not itself the problem — the problem is running two contradictory economic systems at once.
